newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Mir crew about to finish unloading freighter.
newsitem.headline: Mir crew about to finish unloading freighter.

text.p: The crew of Russia's troubled Mir space station have almost finished unloading vital equipment from a supply craft and will soon resume training for repair work, the deputy mission chief said on Wednesday.

The unmanned Progress craft contains oxygen, food, water and tools needed to restore the power supply from energy-generating solar panels on the Spektr module, which was damaged last month when another Russian supply ship hit the ageing space station.

"The guys have almost finished unloading the cargo ship. They are asking us during radio contacts what they have to take out first and what they may leave there," Sergei Krikalyov, the deputy mission chief, told reporters.

Unloading is running ahead of a provisional schedule. Space officials said on Tuesday it would take the two Russian cosmonauts and British-American astronaut up to three days to unload the freighter. Work started on Tuesday morning.
Itar-Tass news agency quoted other officials as saying the work would be completed by the end of the day.
Krikalyov said that after unloading, the cosmonauts would return to checking their spacesuits and to training, which includes a simulation of what they would have to do during repair work.

They will need to attach 17 internal cables to connections inside Spektr. The crew had to disconnect the cables and close the hatch leading to the module after the collision. Three of the four solar panels attached like wings to Spektr are running idle. The fourth panel is unlikely to be repaired.
Mir lost up to half its electric power in the June 25 collision, and a failure to beef up power supplies would threaten the future of the 11-year-old space station.
Interfax news agency said repairs to the power supply were crucial for the arrival of a fresh three-strong crew and joint work by six cosmonauts on board the station.

It quoted Konstantin Lantratov of the Khrunichev design centre, the maker of Mir, as saying the activities of two crews working simultaneously required too much electricity, which even under normal conditions could lead to battery discharge.

He said in 1994 a joint six-strong crew had to work without the light in three modules and with controls partly switched off. Contact with mission control was then maintained through a civilian-type transceiver, brought to Mir by one of the cosmonauts.
Russian cosmonauts Vasily Tsibliyev and Alexander Lazutkin will enter the Spektr in spacesuits to repair the power supply, probably around July 17 or 18.
Their U.S. colleague, British-born Michael Foale, will sit in the Soyuz escape capsule for safety during the repair work, which is expected to last up to four hours.

Two Russians, Anatoly Solovyov and Pavel Vingradov, and Frenchman Leopold Eyharts are due to arrive on Mir in August. All six will work on the staion for three weeks, before Lazutkin and Tsibliyev go back to Earth in a Soyuz craft.
Foale will be picked up from Mir by a U.S. space shuttle in September.
